propositions.statement_en: Ibn Kathir explains the prayer command as directing obligatory and optional prayer solely and sincerely to the Lord.
Ibn Kathir explains sacrifice as performed solely for the Lord and in his name.
Ibn Kathir attributes to Ibn Abbas the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to Ata the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to Mujahid the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to Ikrima the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to al-Hasan the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to Qatada the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to Muhammad ibn Kab al-Qurazi the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to al-Dahhak the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to al-Rabi the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to Ata al-Khurasani the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to al-Hakam the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir attributes to Ismail ibn Abi Khalid the interpretation of the sacrifice command as slaughter of al-budn and similar animals.
Ibn Kathir reports from Ali an interpretation of wanhar as placing the right hand over the left beneath the upper chest.
Ibn Kathir reports a similar hand-placement interpretation from al-Shabi.
Ibn Kathir states that the attribution of this interpretation to Ali does not hold.
Ibn Kathir reports from Abu Jafar al-Baqir an interpretation of wanhar as raising both hands at the opening of prayer.
Ibn Kathir records an unnamed interpretation of wanhar as facing the qibla with one's upper chest.
Ibn Kathir states that Ibn Jarir mentioned these three interpretations.
Ibn Kathir reports from Ata al-Khurasani an interpretation of wanhar as raising and straightening the back after bowing and bringing the upper chest forward.
Ibn Kathir identifies the first interpretation as correct: nahr means slaughtering sacrificial animals.
Ibn Jarir identifies as correct the interpretation that all prayer is to be devoted exclusively to the Lord, excluding other rivals and deities.
Ibn Jarir likewise interprets the sacrifice as being devoted to the Lord rather than idols.
The quoted interpretation presents this as gratitude for the honor and good uniquely bestowed on the addressee, described as without equivalent.
Ibn Kathir commends the preceding interpretation quoted from Ibn Jarir as exceptionally good.
Ibn Kathir states that Muhammad ibn Kab al-Qurazi and Ata had preceded Ibn Jarir in this meaning.
Ibn Kathir describes this particular report as munkar jiddan.
In the report, Muhammad asks Gabriel what the sacrifice commanded by his Lord means.
Within the report, Gabriel denies that the command means a sacrifice.
Within the report, Gabriel says the addressee is commanded, on entering prayer, to raise both hands at takbir, bowing, raising the head from bowing, and prostrating.
Within the report, Gabriel describes this as our prayer and the prayer of the angels in the seven heavens.
Within the report, Gabriel says that everything has an adornment.
Within the report, Gabriel describes raising both hands at every takbir as the adornment of prayer.
In the report attributed through the printed chain to Ali ibn Abi Talib, the subsequent exchange is situated when this surah was revealed to Muhammad; the passage quotes 108:1–2.
Ibn Kathir states that al-Hakim likewise reported it in al-Mustadrak through Israil ibn Hatim, referring back with bihi.
The quoted statement accepts sacrifice performed with the prayer and sacrifice sequence described, and denies ritual validity to sacrifice before the prayer.
Abu Burda says he slaughtered his sheep before the prayer, knowing that meat was desired that day.
The reply characterizes Abu Burda's sheep as a sheep for meat.
Abu Burda asks whether a young female goat he values more than two sheep will suffice for him.
The reply permits it for Abu Burda and states that it will not suffice for anyone after him.
In Ibn Kathir's account, Muhammad would perform the Eid prayer and then slaughter his sacrificial animal.
